categories.label: JIT Delivery Coordination Mechanisms and Compensation Models
categories.memo: Focuses on the operational-contractual problem of achieving just-in-time delivery between independent for-profit factories/suppliers and general contractors, and the compensation/incentive mechanisms proposed to align behaviour.

codes.label: Structural Barrier to Natural JIT Between Independent Entities
codes.description: Because factories/manufacturers and contractors are separate profit-making organisations, JIT delivery cannot occur naturally without explicit financial/contractual mechanisms.

codes.label: Static Compensation Systems Misallocate Risk
codes.description: Existing fixed-price or lump-sum compensation for schedule/delivery changes place all risk of demand fluctuation on the supplier/factory and fail to reflect real-time cost impacts.

codes.label: Dynamic/Quantitative Compensation Mechanisms
codes.description: Proposed dynamic surcharge/incentive systems, rebates, or shared information platforms that quantify real-time cost impact of delivery date changes to better balance risk and incentivise coordination.

codes.label: Contracts as Rigid Push Mechanisms Instead of Coordination Tools
codes.description: Contracts intended to pull components from factories instead force rigid compliance, causing both sides to handle variations unilaterally rather than collaboratively; original contracts remain binding fallback absent negotiated win-win.

codes.label: Schedule Float as a Tradable Contractual Resource
codes.description: Contractor schedule float/slack can be strategically traded for financial incentives from suppliers, subject to precedence relationships and contractually specified maximum allowances for date changes.

codes.label: Contractual Rebate/Penalty Structures for Delivery Adherence
codes.description: Rebate mechanisms rewarding contractors for honoring originally scheduled deliveries, or penalty clauses tied to unit costs of early/late delivery, used to discourage opportunistic rescheduling.

codes.label: Supplier Selection Beyond Lowest Tender
codes.description: Quality-price based supplier selection mechanisms (rather than lowest bid) combined with contractual delivery obligations support JIT implementation.

categories.label: Transportation, Warehousing, and Logistics Optimization
categories.memo: Covers the physical and planning challenges of moving prefabricated components/modules from factory to site, including scheduling optimization, storage constraints, and cost trade-offs.

codes.label: On-Site Storage and Inventory Waste
codes.description: Limited on-site warehouse capacity forces reliance on costly third-party storage; significant waste occurs when delivered components sit unused for extended periods before assembly.

codes.label: Early vs Late Delivery Trade-offs and Penalties
codes.description: Early delivery causes inventory costs, double handling and site congestion; late delivery causes economic and reputational harm; unit penalty costs shape contractor trade-off decisions between punctuality and cost savings.

codes.label: Optimization Models for Delivery Scheduling
codes.description: Mathematical/constraint-programming optimization methods for module transport planning can substantially reduce costs compared to intuitive, experience-based planning used in current practice.

codes.label: Transportation as a Major Cost and Regulatory Constraint
codes.description: Transportation of oversized/heavy modules ranks among top project cost contributors and is complicated by road network constraints, permits, and special traffic controls, especially in dense urban areas.

codes.label: Site Access and Vertical Logistics for High-Rise/Dense Sites
codes.description: Crane operations, vertical transportation, restricted site layouts and site access constrain modular delivery and installation logistics, particularly for high-rise modular projects.

codes.label: Contract-Derived Constraints on Assembly Scheduling
codes.description: Contractually specified field erection deadlines and expected delivery times impose hard constraints on module fabrication/assembly completion timing.

categories.label: Third-Party Logistics and Coordinated Logistics Services
categories.memo: Addresses the role of third-party logistics providers and construction logistics service (CLS) modules, including how their use is contractually mandated and coordinated among multiple actors.

codes.label: Contractual Mandating of Logistics Service Use
codes.description: Subcontractors are often required by contract terms with the main contractor to use specific construction logistics service (CLS) modules, sometimes as non-voluntary users driven by municipal/developer demands.

codes.label: Modularisation of Logistics Services Increases Coordination Complexity
codes.description: Simplifying logistics service content into modules does not simplify overall value co-creation, since more actors and multiple TPL providers must be coordinated, risking lack of coordination between service modules.

codes.label: Main Contractor's Dual Role as Customer and Enforcer
codes.description: The main contractor simultaneously acts as a customer of logistics services and as the party persuading/enforcing subcontractor adoption and payment for mandated services.

codes.label: Temporary Project Organisation Limits Standardization Benefits
codes.description: Because construction actors form temporary organisations per project, trust and coordination mechanisms for logistics services must be rebuilt each time, limiting benefits of standardized logistics arrangements.

categories.label: Fragmentation, Trust, and Coordination Failures in the Off-Site Supply Chain
categories.memo: Covers the relational and organisational barriers—mistrust, fragmentation, risk transfer upstream—that undermine coordination between GCs, subcontractors, manufacturers and factories.

codes.label: Fragmentation Between Off-Site Fabrication and On-Site Assembly
codes.description: Poor collaboration and information sharing between contractors and factories creates a complex, hard-to-manage supply chain, exacerbated by non-conventional connections and multidisciplinary coordination needs.

codes.label: Mistrustful/Adversarial GC-Subcontractor/Supplier Relationships
codes.description: General contractors and subcontractors/suppliers often have conflicting, mistrustful relationships, with risk tending to be transferred upstream toward suppliers, eroding trust and reliability.

codes.label: Disproportionate Risk Borne by Suppliers/Fabricators
codes.description: Off-site suppliers and fabricators bear disproportionate schedule, financial, and delivery risk in the supply chain compared to contractors, who act primarily as purchasers under onerous subcontract terms.

codes.label: Communication Breakdowns and Design Change Disruption
codes.description: Design changes not communicated to downstream manufacturers/factories, obsolete communication methods, and mismatches between design intent and delivered product disrupt manufacturing schedules and cause cost/quality issues.

codes.label: Multi-Project Resource Competition at Manufacturers
codes.description: Manufacturers serving multiple clients/projects simultaneously face resource competition that can delay delivery on any single contracted project.

categories.label: Information Systems and BIM for Supply Chain Coordination
categories.memo: Covers the role of shared information platforms and BIM in enabling visibility, communication and coordination across fragmented off-site/on-site supply chains.

codes.label: Shared Information Platforms for Real-Time Coordination
codes.description: Information technology and shared information systems enable real-time visibility of production status, supporting coordination of delivery date changes between contractors and factories despite financial independence.

codes.label: BIM as a Coordination and Communication Tool
codes.description: BIM supports DfMA/PPVC by enabling digital product data exchange between design and manufacturing, bridging communication gaps and enhancing interdisciplinary coordination, and correlates with greater vendor collaboration.

categories.label: Early Supply Chain Integration and Stakeholder Involvement
categories.memo: Covers the timing and structure of stakeholder involvement—suppliers, manufacturers, vendors, subcontractors—in design and planning phases, and how procurement/contract type shapes this integration.

codes.label: Early Supplier/Manufacturer Involvement in Design
codes.description: Early involvement of suppliers, timber fabricators, or vendors in design—even without formal contractual obligation—improves design feasibility, reduces corrections, and is associated with prefabrication success.

codes.label: Procurement/Contract Type Shapes Collaboration Quality
codes.description: Integrated delivery methods (Design-Build, IPD) outperform traditional Design-Bid-Build for collaboration and coordination in prefabrication/timber/off-site projects; IPD better accommodates off-site prefabrication needs.

codes.label: Networked Rather Than Linear Supply Chain Structure
codes.description: Timber/construction supply chains function as networks with feedback loops between design and construction actors rather than strictly linear sequences, partly to manage risk of unfamiliar materials/methods.

codes.label: Vendor Partnership Agreements as Quasi-Contractual Mechanisms
codes.description: Legally nonbinding vendor partnership agreements formalize mutual responsibilities (communication, delivery, JIT, training) supporting prefabrication coordination absent full contractual binding.

codes.label: Early Decision-Making and Design Freeze Trade-offs
codes.description: Early decisions to adopt modular/prefabricated methods and early design freeze are essential for success but increase risk for the design team due to reduced flexibility for later changes.

categories.label: Financial and Commercial Risk Allocation in Off-Site Supply Chains
categories.memo: Covers financial instruments, cost/margin distribution, and risk-sharing arrangements between builders, suppliers, subcontractors and manufacturers in off-site/prefabricated supply chains.

codes.label: Financial Risk-Mitigation Instruments in Supplier Contracts
codes.description: Use of bank guarantees, insurance certificates, joint trading accounts, and nominated subcontractor arrangements to manage cash flow and delivery risk between builders and off-site suppliers.

codes.label: Onerous/Rigid Subcontract Terms Imposed on Suppliers
codes.description: Large Tier 1 builders impose rigid delivery obligations on suppliers regardless of circumstances, and variation orders disrupt supplier production cycles and coordination without adequate compensation.

codes.label: Cost/Margin Redistribution and Subcontractor Incentive Erosion
codes.description: Prefabrication cost savings tend to be captured by head/main contractors rather than passed to subcontractors, reducing subcontractor scope, margins, and incentive to collaborate; traditional subcontracts lack relational mechanisms needed for benefit-sharing.

codes.label: Multiple/Redundant Supply Arrangements as Risk Mitigation
codes.description: Builders engage duplicate or competing suppliers for the same scope as a contractual risk mitigation strategy against delay or non-performance.

codes.label: High Switching Costs Limiting Market Discipline Over Suppliers
codes.description: Difficulty and cost of switching prefabrication suppliers/fabricators limits contractors' ability to discipline supplier behaviour through competition, reinforcing need for coordinating contract terms.

codes.label: Upfront Capital and Financing Risk for Off-Site Capacity
codes.description: Contractors' and manufacturers' willingness/ability to invest upfront capital in prefabrication facilities affects adoption; modular construction carries higher financing risk due to lender concerns about manufacturer solvency.

categories.label: Labor and Workforce Considerations in Off-Site Supply Chains
categories.memo: Covers union relations, workforce deskilling, and labor-related contractual/coordination issues arising from splitting work between off-site fabrication and on-site installation.

codes.label: Union Resistance and Labor Portability Constraints
codes.description: Local labor union resistance can constrain contractors' ability to prefabricate/outsource building systems off-site, with differentiated resistance depending on whether fabrication is in-house or outsourced.

codes.label: Deskilling and Workforce Planning Risk
codes.description: Shifting trade work to off-site factories risks deskilling tradespeople/apprentices and requires more intricate workforce planning since management staffing needs remain constant despite reduced on-site labor needs.

categories.label: Cross-Jurisdictional and Overseas Manufacturing Coordination
categories.memo: Covers the added complexity of coordinating supply chains where fabrication occurs overseas or across borders, including customs, shipping, and capacity constraints.

codes.label: Overseas/Cross-Border Manufacturing Dependency
codes.description: Reliance on overseas or cross-border manufacturing facilities (due to limited local industrial capacity) increases shipping cost, customs uncertainty, and project complexity.
